target_customer: Bloggers, content sellers, charities and Twitter users who wanted to receive or send small payments
problem: Paying a few cents for online content or tipping a creator was impractical because card and PayPal fees and checkout friction exceeded the amounts.
business_model: Payments aggregation with a small fee per transaction

founders.name: Ivan Kirigin
founders.background_notes: Later hired by Facebook after a failed acquisition, later at Dropbox, and founded YesGraph (W15).

exit.reason: Company announced it would not continue seeking funding after a Facebook acquisition did not complete; collections were turned off while users could cash out.

competitors.name: TipIt.To
competitors.what: Tipping service with a similar model

competitors.name: PayPal donation buttons
competitors.what: Incumbent tip jar and donation payments
competitors.traction_then: ubiquitous but with high fees on small amounts

competitors.name: Tipjar.com
competitors.what: The original TipJar tipping service, not live at the time, with a transaction service relaunch tentatively scheduled for later in 2007

technical_complexity.rationale: Aggregating tiny payments and paying out via Amazon gift cards or charity is standard engineering, but handling money and fraud at small scale added complexity.

defensibility.rationale: Easily copied by PayPal, Twitter payment apps and rivals; no network effect beyond Twitter integration.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Facebook explored buying it, backed away in 2009 and hired Ivan Kirigin instead.

market_need_then: Bloggers and Twitter users wanted a low friction way to reward content, shown by press about tipping tools in early 2008, but willingness to tip proved small.

identity.voice_and_tone: Casual and friendly, founders ran a personal blog called Tipjoy's 2 cents

branding.brand_signature: Tip Me button for websites and Twitter
branding.community_and_virality: Popular among early Twitter users and covered by TechCrunch and Readwrite.

brand_strength.rationale: Memorable name and active in early Twitter circles, but little evidence of broad awareness.

pivots.from: Tip jar for content and Twitter
pivots.to: Selling digital content and features with checkout
pivots.why: Company blog announced selling digital content as a way to expand use beyond tips.

outcome_analysis: Tipjoy raised about 1M USD in September 2008, rode early Twitter popularity, but struggled to turn tipping into meaningful volume. In August 2009 it shut down collections after deciding not to keep raising and after Facebook backed away from a full acquisition, hiring the CTO instead. Small payment size and weak tipping behavior limited revenue.
notes: Company website did not resolve (DNS failure), treated as dead. CB Insights lists about 2M USD across four rounds with unmatched dates; unverified. Xconomy and CBS both support the 1M USD round. Search snippets for the shutdown and Facebook stories came from TechCrunch headlines; details beyond headlines were summarized by the search tool. Failure causes are inferred from those reports and are partly judgment. Audit fix: the 1M round of 2008-09 is now stage seed because it was Tipjoy's first outside round. CB Insights lists about 2M over four rounds with unmatched dates, which would imply more funding than the one recorded round; that is unverified and not recorded. Tipjar.com is added as a competitor from The Next Web (2008-02-13), which describes it as not live.
